what_source_says: Wannigama (public UNSW dataset, ref. Sivanathan TMC, 'originally collected in 2016'): Awair had 647 TLS flows on TCP/443 [+179 on other ports], always offered and got TLS 1.2, no ClientHello extensions; its servers selected 0x003c and 0x003d (TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256 / TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256) and 'consistently chose a weak code from the client-suggested ciphersuite' (weak per ciphersuite.info). Loi 2017 (UNSW lab): Awair device-to-server not plaintext, protocol SSL, entropy 7.89; fake server 'Fail SSL'. TSM 2018: Awair confidentiality rated A.
difference: Ours: 826 handshakes, 744 TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA256 and 82 TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256, no forward secrecy, against the support article 'Awair encrypts and stores all information over TLS ... and AES 256 bit encryption' (2016-07). Wannigama's counts (647+179=826) and suites match ours, so likely the same raw traces (inference). They label the suites 'weak' but do not discuss AES-128 vs AES-256, forward secrecy by name, or the vendor claim.
queries: Q1: "Awair" air quality monitor security TLS cipher suite analysis | Q2: "Awair" vulnerability OR CVE OR "forward secrecy" OR "AES 256" IoT device | Q3: IoT vendor claims "AES 256" but TLS negotiates AES-128 without forward secrecy measurement paper | Q4: "Awair" IoT device paper "SSL" OR "TLS" encryption evaluation UNSW smart home | (Wannigama found via the SmartCam query Q5; venue via Crossref API)
notes: Contradiction itself: not found. Communication problem (server-chosen RSA suites without forward secrecy, mostly AES-128): in a non-top paper (WoWMoM). No top-4 paper names Awair (prior-tls.tsv NOT-IN-MATRIX). Conference version text not read (arXiv full version read). No Awair CVE found.

what_source_says: Bradley: a D-Link device in Ren's lab ('movement sensor' in §3.3, 'camera' in §4.1) asks an HTTP update web service that 'accepts a device model' and returns XML with an HTTP S3 firmware URL; no checksum or signature; no MAC or device ID mentioned. Threatpost 2016: mydlink agent registers device ID and MAC over TLS with weak settings (SSLv23, no certificate check). ESET 2019 (DCS-2132L): camera IP and MAC unencrypted in the tunnel. Sources cover other models (motion sensor, cameras) and earlier years; none names this host, DCH-S161, or the MAC in an update check; none compares with the privacy-policy SSL sentence. what_source_says: AV-TEST blog 2019 (Roomba 980, iRobot app 3.2.0): 'all local communication was TLS1.2 encrypted'; the robot 'always communicates TLS1.2 encrypted'; 'Unencrypted connections could not be detected'; conclusion 'a secure solution for both local network and cloud communication'. No cipher suite or key length. AV-TEST news 2019-01-30: iRobot relies on TLS 1.2 for the cloud and the app; no key length. Alrawi (same YourThings unit, 2018): device-cloud encryption full (filled circle), MITM x on D-C, A-C, A-D; no cipher data. dorita980: the robot's own local MQTT/TLS server (LAN) - default cipher 'AES128-SHA256'. openHAB: 'Some Roomba models use an outdated TLS configuration and require the legacy cipher TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA' (local connection to the robot; models not named).
difference: Ours: all 34 handshakes chose AES-128-GCM (TLS 1.3 TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 20, TLS 1.2 ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 14), against 'Currently, we use AES 256-bit encryption and Transport Layer Security (TLS v1.2).' (iRobot data-security page, archived 2021-12-06). No source gives the cipher of Roomba's connections to the cloud; AV-TEST gives only the TLS version (1.2). The GitHub/openHAB notes are about the robot's local MQTT server (another path) and show both AES-128 and AES-256 suites, depending on the model.
queries: Q1: iRobot Roomba network traffic TLS MQTT security analysis paper | Q2: Roomba "AES 256" "TLS" iRobot encryption claim traffic cipher suite AES-128 | Q3: robot vacuum security privacy analysis iRobot Roomba TLS cloud communication cipher USENIX OR WOOT OR "IEEE" paper | Q4: "So fresh, so clean" cloud forensic analysis iRobot Roomba Forensic Science International Digital Investigation 2024 | Q5: iRobot Roomba vulnerability CVE TLS OR encryption OR "man-in-the-middle" cloud i7 OR 980 OR j7 advisory | cached papers (prior-cache/prior-academic) grepped for roomba/irobot: alrawi, pingpong, ahmed, iotfinder, mazhar, prakash - none gives Roomba ciphers
notes: Contradiction itself (AES-256 claim vs AES-128 negotiated): not found. Communication problem itself: AES-128-GCM with forward secrecy (and TLS 1.3, newer than the stated 1.2) is not a weakness; the gap is only the stated key length, and no source reports Roomba cloud cipher suites at all; local path only in GitHub/docs. Not NG-top: Alrawi (S&P) has no cipher data. Unread (未確認): Onik, Alsmadi, Baggili, Webb, 'So fresh, so clean: Cloud forensic analysis of the Amazon iRobot Roomba vacuum', FSI: Digital Investigation 48 (2024) 301686 (DFRWS EU) - DFRWS PDF returned 403, topic per search result is cloud/app API forensics; Ullrich et al., 'Vacuums in the Cloud', WOOT 2019 - search result says Neato/Vorwerk, not read; Ulsmaag et al., arXiv 2407.18433 (ICICS 2024) - abstract page does not name the vacuum; K. what_source_says: Mandalari: non-required destinations 'consistently use HTTPS (TCP/443), with just the following exceptions: two domains using HTTP (TCP/80) (fireoscaptiveportal.com and diagnostics.meethue.com)'; Table 8 lists dcp.dc1.philips.com, ws.meethue.com (required) and diagnostics.meethue.com, ecdinterface.philips.com (non-required); contents not analysed. AV-TEST 2017: 'almost all communication [Bridge-Philips servers] is performed over HTTP', payload encrypted 'separately with AES'; judged 'adequately secure'; suspects hard-coded keys. Amar 2018: Hue Bridge and Neato 'communicate via plain HTTP with other devices and the outside world'; the Hue details shown are LAN (API keys sniffed from app-bridge traffic); the bridge only DNS-queried www.ecdinterface.philips.com and did not connect to it. Alrawi: Philips HUE device-cloud encryption full (filled circle). IoT Inspector: 85.4% of 355 'philips' devices (98.3% named hue) talked to non-tracking hosts on port 80 (vendor level, no payload). SIDN 2020: contacts meethue.com, philips.com, Google NTP; connectivity checks carry no HTTP data; protocol of the rest not stated. SSTIC 2026: LAN HomeKit (HAP) and Zigbee bugs; not the cloud path.
difference: Ours: 27% of the bridge's traffic is plaintext HTTP: POST diagnostics.meethue.com/v2/diagnostics/report?report_type=...&sso=<token> (hex ciphertext body), POST dcp.dc1.philips.com:80/DcpRequestHandler/index.ashx with 'Authorization: CBAuth' carrying the bridge id and an SSO token; against 'Hue only connects to the internet securely via a dedicated cloud so your devices cannot be seen from the open internet.' (FAQ, archived 2021-12-22). Sources report HTTP to Philips hosts (blog 2017; PoPETs 2021 for diagnostics.meethue.com), but none shows the sso token or the bridge id in clear, and none compares the traffic with this FAQ. AV-TEST called the same HTTP+AES design 'adequately secure', so a contradiction of 'securely' rests on the ids and tokens sent in clear, not on HTTP alone.

what_source_says: OConnor 2019 (NCSU lab): TuyaSmart Motion Sensor uses 'MQTT, HTTP' (MQTT-S is listed only for other devices) and its alerts were blocked by matching 'PROTOCOL == MQTT AND PAYLOAD CONTAINS "out"' (so the MQTT text was readable: our reading); the Merkury camera sent motion notifications 'over a plain-text MQTT connection'; identifiers not discussed. Girish 2023: Tuya devices' DHCP hostnames contain a partial MAC; on the LAN (TuyaLP, UDP 6666/6667) 'The Jinvoo Bulb sends its GWid and Product key in plaintext'. Jia slides: Tuya Smart uses application-layer encryption with a key updated per user; impersonation by keeping an MQTT session; ClientIds are often a MAC or serial and 'not a secret'; transport encryption not stated. HITCON 2018 (a Tuya plug): MQTT payload 'somehow encrypted'; 'device sends devID and a password as MQTT username/password'; pairing uses HTTP 'POST /gw.json?a=s.gw.token.get', 's.gw.dev.pk.active' (returns the localKey), 's.gw.update'. HA forum 2017: Tuya switches use HTTPS and MQTT, 'The traffic is mostly non-SSL, except when the app grabs device info (local key)'; a LAN query in plain text carries devId/gwId 002006615ccf7fe01925 (last 12 hex 5ccf7fe01925; 5CCF7F is in tuya-convert's Espressif OUI list). tuya-convert: the fake cloud reads a, et and gwId from the /gw.json query, the body is hex AES (et=1) or plain; MQTT broker on 1883 with anonymous access, topic smart/device/in/<gwId>. heise 2019: Tuya says firmware released 2019-01-28 will send data only over TLS; Tuya says AES keys sent in plaintext were fixed in August 2018.
difference: Ours (2018-05..10, before Tuya's January 2019 change): plaintext POST a.tuyaus.com/gw.json with gwId containing the MAC, and plaintext MQTT on tcp/1883 with clientId equal to the same gwId. HITCON 2018, the HA forum and tuya-convert describe the same design (gw.json over HTTP with gwId in the query; MQTT with the device ID), heise reports Tuya's own move to TLS-only, and OConnor shows a Tuya device on MQTT without TLS. None states that the gwId sent to the cloud embeds the MAC (only the forum's example value and Girish's LAN case show MAC-derived IDs), and no top-4 paper reports this for Tuya devices.
